title: Enhanced intrinsic spin-orbit driving of a Loss-DiVincenzo qubit near the spin-valley hotspot in Si/SiGe
authors: Alexander Willmes, Max Oberländer, Max Beer, Denny Dütz, Jhih-Sian Tu, Stefan Trellenkamp, Marco Lisker, Felix Reichmann, Lars R. Schreiber, Hendrik Bluhm
abstract: In most Si/SiGe-based spin qubit implementations, high-fidelity single-qubit gates are achieved using micromagnets, which enable the use of electric spin dipole resonance via synthetic spin-orbit coupling (s-SOC). In contrast, intrinsic spin-orbit coupling (i-SOC) in silicon is generally considered to be weak. However, in Si/SiGe heterostructures, theory predicts a substantial enhancement when the Zeeman splitting approaches the valley splitting if symmetry is reduced by an imperfect interface. Here, we demonstrate a Si/SiGe Loss-DiVincenzo qubit driven by i-SOC close to this so-called spin-valley hotspot. In particular, we characterize the Rabi frequency as a function of the energy detuning from the hotspot by sweeping both the magnetic field and quantum dot position. We observe the predicted enhancement of the Rabi frequency near the hotspot, but also find an asymmetry that deviates from existing theoretical models as well as distortions of the Chevron patterns near the hotspot. While we achieve an average single-qubit Clifford fidelity of 98.6 %, the strong variability of the valley splitting may impede the use of i-SOC-based control as a scalable operational strategy; understanding its effect is nevertheless important for reproducible high-fidelity control. Our results provide an empirical basis for refining current theoretical models of spin-valley physics in Si/SiGe heterostructures.
summary: This experimental work investigates using intrinsic spin-orbit coupling in Si/SiGe qubits to achieve high-fidelity quantum gates near a predicted spin-valley hotspot. While the enhanced Rabi frequency was observed, the study also revealed significant asymmetries and variability, indicating that while the mechanism is confirmed, its practical implementation faces challenges for scalable control.
main_problem: The study aims to demonstrate and characterize the enhanced intrinsic spin-orbit coupling (i-SOC) driving of a Loss-DiVincenzo qubit near a predicted spin-valley hotspot in Si/SiGe heterostructures.
main_result: The researchers observed the predicted enhancement of the Rabi frequency near the hotspot, but also found significant asymmetries and variability, suggesting that i-SOC control is not yet a scalable strategy.
method: The experiment uses microwave pulse sequences and Rabi measurements to probe the qubit dynamics, varying parameters like magnetic field and quantum dot position to map the energy detuning from the hotspot.
model_or_system: The system is a spin qubit implemented in a Si/SiGe heterostructure, utilizing the spin-valley coupling mechanism. The physics is governed by the interplay between Zeeman splitting and valley splitting, leading to the 'hotspot' where hybridization occurs.
key_observables: Rabi frequency ($\Omega_R$), single-qubit Clifford fidelity ($F$), Chevron patterns, and the dependence of resonance frequency on energy detuning ($\Delta E_v$).
important_parameters: The hotspot condition ($\Delta E_v = 0$), the measured spin-valley coupling strength ($|C| \approx 0.75 \mu	ext{eV}$), and the achieved fidelity ($F \approx 98.6\%$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed phenomena are dominated by i-SOC effects near the hotspot, although the variability suggests other noise sources (like nuclear spins) might be at play.
figures_summary: Figures detail Rabi experiments showing Chevron patterns, energy diagrams mapping the anticrossing, and plots showing the Rabi frequency dependence on detuning, alongside coherence time ($T_2^*$) vs. detuning.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from characterizing the basic qubit operation and observing the predicted Rabi enhancement at the hotspot, to detailing the observed asymmetries and limitations, and finally analyzing coherence time and noise susceptibility to constrain theoretical models.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial empirical data on utilizing intrinsic material couplings (i-SOC) for qubit control, directly addressing the feasibility of solid-state quantum computing platforms beyond traditional magnetic control.
